options: It prints an arbitrary value, which is implementation-defined but still defined behavior.
It fails to compile because returning a reference to a local variable is ill-formed in C++.
It compiles but has undefined behavior at runtime because r is a dangling reference to a destroyed local.
It reliably prints 5 because the reference binds to the local variable's memory, which stays valid until after main prints it.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The code compiles, but the function returns a reference to a local variable that is destroyed at the end of bad(). r becomes a dangling reference. Any use of r has undefined behavior.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Tempting because the address might still appear to hold 5 in a trivial run, but the lifetime has ended and UB can manifest unpredictably. C: The language allows forming such a reference; the error is semantic (lifetime), not ill-formed. D: Tempting if one confuses "implementation-defined" with UB; here the behavior is not defined at all.

options: Fails to compile because a reference cannot bind to a temporary.
Prints 4, and it is safe because the temporary's lifetime is extended to match r.
Compiles, but the result is unspecified because temporary lifetime rules only apply to single objects, not the result of operator+.
Prints 4, but it is undefined behavior because the temporary is destroyed before the print.
concept_mcqs.explanation: A const lvalue reference can bind to a temporary, and that temporary's lifetime is extended to the reference's lifetime. The string is "abcd", so size() is 4.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Confuses with non-const references; only const lvalue references extend lifetime. C: A common misconception; binding to temporaries is allowed for const lvalue refs. D: Operator+ yields a temporary just like any other expression; lifetime extension still applies.

options: long
int
Undefined behavior due to signedness mismatch on promotion
Ambiguous: both are viable with equal rank
concept_mcqs.explanation: short promotes to int via integral promotion, which is a better conversion than conversion to long. So f(int) is selected.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Tempting if one thinks widening to long is always preferred; integral promotion to int is a higher-ranked conversion. C: Both are viable, but not equal rank; promotion beats conversion. D: Signedness is well-defined on promotion; no UB here.

concept_mcqs.explanation: Default arguments are bound statically at the call site based on the static type (Base), so 1 is passed. The function call itself is virtual, so Derived::f is invoked with x=1, printing D:1.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Assumes both default arg and virtual dispatch are dynamic; only the function selection is dynamic. C/D: Misunderstand that the object is a Derived and the call is virtual; Base's body isn't called.

options: It alternates between B and D across runs
B
Undefined behavior because of slicing
D
concept_mcqs.explanation: Passing by value slices the derived part off, creating a separate B subobject. The virtual call on that B object dispatches to B::who, printing B.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Would be true if passing by reference/pointer. C: Slicing is defined behavior (just likely incorrect), not UB. D: There is no nondeterminism here; dispatch is statically well-defined after slicing.

options: It prints only ~B, but this is still well-defined.
It prints ~B~D because destructors chain automatically.
It fails to compile because delete requires a virtual destructor.
It has undefined behavior; typically you'll only see ~B printed.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Deleting through a base pointer without a virtual destructor is undefined behavior. In many builds you will observe only B's destructor run, leaking D's resources, but the behavior is not defined.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Destructors only chain correctly when the base has a virtual destructor and deletion is through that base. B: Observed behavior isn't guaranteed; it's UB. D: The code compiles; virtual is a runtime mechanism, not a compile-time requirement for delete.

options: Compile error because the compiler enforces initializer list order.
Well-defined, prints 42 because y is initialized from x after x becomes 42.
Well-defined, prints an unspecified but valid value because y copies from default-initialized x.
Undefined behavior because y is initialized from an indeterminate x; declaration order controls initialization.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Members are initialized in declaration order, not the order written in the initializer list. x is indeterminate when y(x) runs. Using that indeterminate value is undefined behavior.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Confuses list order with initialization order. B: Suggests "unspecified but defined"; reading an indeterminate int is UB. D: Compilers accept the code; they don't reorder based on the list, they follow declaration order silently.

options: Fails to compile because Der may access Base::v only through a Der (or further-derived) object, not an arbitrary Base.
Compiles only if g is marked friend of Base.
Compiles and sets b.v to 5 because Der can access Base's protected members.
Runs but is undefined behavior due to violating access control at runtime.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Protected allows access within Der to Base's protected members on a Der (or further-derived) object. Accessing through a plain Base object b is ill-formed, so the code fails to compile.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Protected isn't the same as "public to derived for all objects"; it is restricted to the derived's subobjects. C: Access control is a compile-time rule, not UB. D: A friend declaration would be in Base, not by marking g; and friendship isn't required for correct derivation-based access.

options: B, because D does not override f(double); the call resolves to B::f(double).
D, because virtual dispatch chooses D for any f.
Undefined behavior because the name f is hidden in D.
Ambiguous call because both f(int) and f(double) are viable.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The static type at the call site is B*, so lookup finds B::f(double). D does not override that signature, so the virtual call targets B::f(double), printing B.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Virtual dispatch only applies among overrides with the same signature. C: Overload set is from B at this call site; D::f(int) is not considered. D: Name hiding is a lookup effect, not UB.

options: Undefined behavior because references cannot be reassigned after binding.
Compiles and r becomes a reference to x inside S's constructor.
Fails to compile because reference members must be bound in the initializer list.
Compiles but r dangles after the constructor because x is destroyed.
concept_mcqs.explanation: A reference member must be bound during member initialization; by the time the constructor body runs, r is uninitialized and cannot be assigned to bind it. The code is ill-formed.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Misunderstands that assignment in the body can bind a reference; it only assigns to the referent if already bound. B: Invents a temporary x; there is no such parameter-lifetime issue here. D: UB is the wrong category; the compiler rejects it.

scenario_questions.task: Diagnose the failure precisely and propose two safe, idiomatic fixes. For each fix, provide the corrected function signature and one-line rationale about performance and lifetime. Mention any relevant C++ guarantees that make the fix acceptable.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
- Problem: `a + b` creates a temporary `std::string`. Returning a const reference binds to that temporary, which is destroyed at the end of `join`, leaving a dangling reference. Using `r` is undefined behavior.

Two fixes:
1) Return by value (relying on NRVO/move elision):
```cpp
std::string join(const std::string& a, const std::string& b) {
    return a + b; // copy elision/move makes this efficient
}
```
Rationale: The returned prvalue constructs the result directly in the caller (copy elision is mandatory in C++17 for prvalues), giving a self-contained string with correct lifetime.

2) Output parameter bound by non-const reference:
```cpp
void join(const std::string& a, const std::string& b, std::string& out) {
    out = a + b;
}
```
Rationale: The caller supplies storage and controls the lifetime of `out`. No dangling; assignment is explicit and efficient. Choose this when you want to reuse an existing buffer.

Either way, do not return a reference to a temporary.

rubric.criterion: Identifies dangling reference to a temporary and explains the lifetime issue
Provides a correct return-by-value solution with performance rationale (NRVO/move elision)
Provides a correct out-parameter solution with rationale about caller-managed lifetime
Uses precise C++ terms (temporary, prvalue, lifetime) and avoids incorrect claims

rubric.criterion: Accurately describes declaration-order initialization and its consequence here
Provides a correct, minimal fix with reordered initializers that yields well-defined behavior
States the language rule about member initialization order explicitly

practical_tasks.title: Build a numeric stats CLI using functions, control flow, and references

practical_tasks.title: Polymorphic shape reporter using classes, constructors, inheritance, and virtual functions
practical_tasks.brief:
Implement a CLI shapes that reads one shape description per line from stdin and prints its name and area. Supported inputs:
- rect w h
- circle r
- tri b h
For each line, construct an object of the corresponding derived class on the stack, then pass it by reference to a function that accepts a Shape& and prints the result. Do not store shapes; process each line as it arrives. Use proper constructors to initialize dimensions, validate arguments (>0), and use virtual dispatch to compute area.
practical_tasks.deliverable: Source file main.cpp that builds with: g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic main.cpp -o shapes, plus a README.txt describing supported inputs and examples.
acceptance_criteria: Defines an abstract base class Shape with: virtual ~Shape() = default; virtual const char* name() const = 0; virtual double area() const = 0;
Implements Rectangle, Circle, Triangle with appropriate constructors initializing their dimensions; members are private with access via const-qualified methods.
Validation: if any dimension <= 0, print an error to stderr for that line and skip output for it.
Implements a function `report(Shape&)` that prints: `name=..., area=...` with area to 3 decimal places.
Uses dynamic polymorphism via a Shape& parameter; no global state; no containers or dynamic allocation required.

Exact sample behavior:
```text
Input:
rect 3 4
circle 2
tri 3 5
tri -1 2
Output:
name=Rectangle, area=12.000
name=Circle, area=12.566
name=Triangle, area=7.500
```
Compiles cleanly with the provided flags.

rubric.criterion: Correct class design (abstract base with virtual destructor and pure virtuals; derived classes overriding correctly)
Constructor usage and argument validation; encapsulation and const-correctness
Polymorphic reporting via Shape& with correct formatting and per-line processing (no unnecessary storage)
Input parsing robustness and error handling for invalid dimensions or tokens
Build quality (compiles cleanly with warnings enabled)

options: Undefined behavior because `std::sort` moves elements and the comparator may dereference moved-from `unique_ptr`s.
Prints the pointer addresses unsorted because the comparator compares ownership, not values.
Compilation error because `std::sort` requires copyable elements and `std::unique_ptr` is non-copyable.
concept_mcqs.explanation: `std::unique_ptr` is MoveConstructible and MoveAssignable, which is sufficient for `std::sort`. The comparator dereferences the `unique_ptr`s and compares the pointed-to ints, producing a sorted sequence by value. No dereference of moved-from pointers occurs inside the comparator; the comparator only sees references to elements at the time of comparison. Output is `1 2 3 `.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
- B is tempting because many remember non-copyable types can be problematic with algorithms, but `std::sort` only needs movable elements in modern C++.
- C sounds plausible if one conflates element moves with comparator arguments, but the comparator receives references to valid elements during comparisons.
- D would be true if the comparator compared the raw pointer addresses (or defaulted to pointer comparison), but the comparator dereferences and compares the ints.

options: Undefined behavior because the `push_back` may reallocate and invalidate `it`.
It reliably prints `30` because the vector grows and shifts elements.
A standard exception is thrown due to iterator invalidation.
It reliably prints `10` because the first element did not change.
concept_mcqs.explanation: `v.reserve(2)` sets capacity to 2. The third `push_back` forces a reallocation, invalidating all iterators, including `it`. Dereferencing an invalidated iterator is undefined behavior. The standard does not specify an exception for this case.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
- A is a common misconception: content stability does not imply iterator validity after reallocation.
- C confuses element movement with deterministic output; even if elements move, the invalidated iterator cannot be trusted.
- D is attractive if one expects runtime checks, but the standard does not require exceptions for iterator invalidation.

options: Runtime double-free because both the `map` and the local `kv` own the same pointer.
Compiles and erases element `1` safely, leaving the map empty.
Undefined behavior due to invalidating the range-for's internal iterator while erasing the current element.
Compilation error because copying `std::pair<const int, std::unique_ptr<int>>` is ill-formed (moves are not used by range-for by value).
concept_mcqs.explanation: The range-based for with `auto kv` copies each element into `kv`. Copying a `std::pair<const int, std::unique_ptr<int>>` tries to copy the `unique_ptr`, which is not allowed. The program does not compile. If written by reference, you'd still have to handle iterator invalidation carefully, but the first failure is at compilation.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
- B is a later-stage problem if the code compiled by reference; it's tempting because erasing while iterating is tricky.
- C assumes associative containers allow safe erase in any context, but ignores the move-only copy issue.
- D is a plausible memory-model fear, but `unique_ptr` is non-copyable precisely to prevent double ownership by copy.

options: They are destroyed only if compiled with optimizations that elide reference counting.
Both `Node` objects are destroyed because they go out of scope at the end of `main`.
Both `Node` objects leak because the reference count cycle prevents destruction; break the cycle with a `std::weak_ptr` on one side.
`a` is destroyed but `b` leaks because its `prev` points to `a`.
concept_mcqs.explanation: `shared_ptr` reference counting cannot reclaim cycles. `a` and `b` keep each other alive via `next`/`prev`. One side should be a `weak_ptr` to break the cycle so that counts can reach zero.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
- B is a naive view of scope-based destruction ignoring shared ownership semantics.
- C imagines asymmetric destruction without addressing the cycle.
- D incorrectly attributes deterministic lifetime to compiler optimizations; reference counting is runtime, not an optimization artefact.

options: It leaks because the `throw` bypasses the `fclose` call.
It is correctly closed via the custom deleter during stack unwinding.
Behavior is undefined because `decltype(&std::fclose)` is not a valid deleter type.
It is closed twice: once by the runtime and once by the custom deleter.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The `unique_ptr`'s destructor runs during stack unwinding and invokes the custom deleter (`fclose`). This is the core of RAII: resources are released when their owners go out of scope, even via exceptions.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
- B is the classic manual-management pitfall; RAII explicitly addresses this.
- C incorrectly assumes an extra close occurs; only the `unique_ptr` manages the resource.
- D is false; a function pointer type to `fclose` is a common and valid `unique_ptr` deleter.

options: Prints `1` because `operator+` on `set` iterators is a no-op.
Prints `2` because advancing by one works on all standard iterators.
Undefined behavior because `operator+` compiles but is invalid for sets.
Compilation error because `std::set` iterators are bidirectional and do not support `operator+`.
concept_mcqs.explanation: `std::set` provides bidirectional iterators that support `++`/`--` but not random-access operations like `it + 1`. The code fails to compile. Use `++it` or `std::next(it)` instead.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
- B confuses iterator categories; only random-access iterators support `+`.
- C suggests a runtime issue, but the operation is ill-formed at compile time.
- D imagines a defined but inert `operator+`; no such operator exists for set iterators.

options:
```text
1 2 2 3 
```
Because erasing by index inside the loop is a no-op.

```text
1 2 3 
```
Because erasing shifts elements left and the loop skips checking the element that shifted into position `i`.
Undefined behavior due to invalidated references from `v[i]` after `erase`.

```text
1 3 
```
Because both even numbers are removed as the loop continues.
concept_mcqs.explanation: After erasing the element at index 1 (the first `2`), the next element (`2`) shifts into index 1. The loop increments `i` to 2 and never checks the new element at index 1. One `2` remains, producing `1 2 3 `.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
- B assumes every even is removed; it ignores the index shift causing a skip.
- C is incorrect; `erase` removes elements and shifts the tail.
- D overstates the hazard: `v[i]` is evaluated only when `i < v.size()` holds; while logic is flawed, no UB occurs here.

options: Undefined behavior because `++it` runs on an invalidated iterator after `erase`.
Well-defined only in debug builds; undefined in release builds.
Well-defined: only the erased iterator is invalidated; the loop removes keys 1 and 3 and ends with `{2:20}`.
Compilation error because `std::map::erase(iterator)` is ambiguous.
concept_mcqs.explanation: In standard C++, `map::erase(it)` invalidates only the erased iterator. But this code then applies `++it` in the loop increment on an invalidated iterator. The safe pattern is `it = m.erase(it)` (C++11 and later) or equivalently increment an iterator saved before erasing.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
- B ignores that the loop increment still uses the old iterator.
- C is false; the overload resolution is not ambiguous here.
- D suggests build-configuration-dependent semantics; iterator validity rules are not conditional on debug builds.

concept_mcqs.explanation: `d1` and `d2` have different (lambda) types; `d2` also captures, so it cannot convert to a plain function pointer. Using `std::function<void(FILE*)>` as the deleter type allows storing both deleters in the same `vector` element type.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
- A uses `decltype(d1)`, which cannot accept `d2` because the types differ.
- B would work for non-capturing lambdas, but `d2` captures and is not convertible to a function pointer.
- D uses the default deleter type and does not match the provided emplace arguments with custom deleters.

options: Undefined behavior because `reserve` does not create elements; indexing past `size()` is invalid.
Well-defined: `reserve` grows the vector so `v[0]` is valid after it.
Compilation error because `operator[]` is deleted for empty vectors.
Throws an exception because bounds are checked in `operator[]`.
concept_mcqs.explanation: `reserve` increases capacity, not size. No elements exist until inserted, so `v[0]` is out of bounds and dereferencing it is undefined behavior. Bounds checking is provided by `at()`, not `operator[]`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
- B confuses capacity with size; `operator[]` is only valid when `0 < size()`.
- C is false; `operator[]` exists but its behavior is undefined out of bounds.
- D describes `at()`, not `operator[]`.

scenario_questions.task: Identify all correctness issues related to ownership and iteration. Propose a corrected implementation that is exception-safe, does not leak, and does not double-delete. Justify each change with the relevant rule (RAII, iterator validity for `vector`, exception safety guarantees).

rubric.criterion: Accurately identifies double-delete from `delete it->get()` and ties it to `unique_ptr` ownership semantics (RAII).
Explains iterator invalidation on `vector::erase` and why `++it` after erase is undefined/incorrect.
Proposes and correctly applies the erase-return iterator pattern, with no manual delete.
Addresses exception safety of `close()` (catch/guarantee, or making it noexcept) and maintains container invariants.

scenario_questions.task: Diagnose the root cause, propose precise changes to break ownership cycles while preserving ability to traverse up and down, and explain how your choice interacts with container behavior (iterator stability, invalidation). Provide brief corrected code fragments.

rubric.criterion: Correctly identifies shared_ptr cycle as the reason memory persists after clearing the index.
Proposes replacing the parent link with `weak_ptr` and justifies ownership direction.
Explains how to use `lock()` for upward traversal, including null-check semantics.

scenario_questions.task: Explain precisely why the crashes occur. Propose two distinct, viable fixes that respect the need for fast later access: one that continues to use `std::vector<int>` and one that changes data representation. For each, explain iterator/reference validity and complexity trade-offs.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
Cause: `std::vector` reallocation on growth invalidates all iterators. The `out` vector stores iterators into `src`; after `src` grows beyond capacity, those iterators dangle, and dereferencing them in `consume` is undefined behavior.

Fix A (stay with `vector`):
- Reserve sufficient capacity in `src` ahead of time (`src.reserve(expected_size)`), or avoid growth between `collect` and `consume`.
- Alternatively, store stable indices (`size_t`) instead of iterators: `out_idx.push_back(static_cast<size_t>(it - src.begin()))`, then dereference via `src[idx]`. Index validity is preserved across reallocation as long as elements are not erased/reordered.

Fix B (change representation):
- Use a node-based container with stable iterators (not covered here beyond `map`/`set`; however within the taught set, prefer storing keys in `std::map` and taking iterators to `map` elements, which remain valid across insertions and do not invalidate other iterators on erase). Re-model data so later access uses `map` (e.g., map from position to value) or keep selected items in a separate `std::vector<int>` copied by value.

Trade-offs:
- Reserving capacity maintains O(1) amortized appends and preserves iterators if no reallocation occurs; but it relies on accurate size prediction.
- Indices are stable across reallocation but break if elements are erased or re-ordered; access remains O(1).
- Using `map` gives stable iterators and ordered traversal but changes complexity of insertion/lookup to O(log n) and increases memory overhead.
- Copying selected values into a separate vector avoids aliasing entirely at the cost of extra storage and possible staleness if `src` mutates later.

rubric.criterion: Explains vector reallocation and iterator invalidation as the root cause.
Proposes an in-vector solution (reserve or indices) with correct validity and complexity discussion.
Proposes an alternative representation (e.g., map or copy-out) with correct validity and complexity discussion.
Notes constraints/limitations of each fix (e.g., erases/reorders break indices; map cost trade-offs).

scenario_questions.scenario:
You are designing a resource registry for a game engine. Each resource has a string key and heavy data. Requirements:
- Iteration must be in key-sorted order.
- Clients obtain handles that can outlive the registry temporarily but must not keep resources alive unnecessarily.
- Multiple clients may reference the same resource concurrently.
- Registry insertions/erasures must not invalidate other clients’ handles.

Two candidate designs:

A)
```cpp
std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::shared_ptr<Resource>>> registry;
// binary-search by key; clients hold std::shared_ptr<Resource>
```

B)
```cpp
std::map<std::string, std::shared_ptr<Resource>> registry;
// clients hold std::weak_ptr<Resource>; registry holds shared_ptr
```
scenario_questions.task: Choose a design (A, B, or a refined variant) and justify it against the requirements. If you modify the design, show the key changes (container choice, pointer types) and explain iterator/handle stability and ownership semantics. Include brief code illustrating safe lookup, handle acquisition, and cleanup.

rubric.criterion: Selects an appropriate container for sorted iteration and explains the choice (map over vector/binary-search).
Justifies `weak_ptr` for client handles and `shared_ptr` in the registry with correct ownership semantics.
Explains iterator and handle stability semantics under insert/erase and how erased entries behave for clients.
Provides clear, correct code illustrating lookup, handle acquisition (lock), and cleanup.

practical_tasks.title: Safe resource exercise: RAII wrapper for FILE* with exception safety
practical_tasks.brief: Build a small C++ library and demo that wraps a C `FILE*` using RAII. The wrapper must manage ownership, support move-only semantics, and guarantee that the file is closed exactly once even if exceptions are thrown during operations. Provide a demo program that intentionally throws after writing to show the destructor still closes the file.
practical_tasks.deliverable: A repository/folder containing: (1) `unique_file.h/.cpp` (or a header-only) implementing the RAII type; (2) `demo.cpp` showing correct behavior under normal flow and when an exception is thrown; (3) a simple build instruction in `README.md` using a standard compiler; and (4) program output captured in `output.txt`.
acceptance_criteria: `UniqueFile` (name may vary) encapsulates a `FILE*` and closes it in the destructor via `std::fclose` or an equivalent custom deleter.
Copy operations are disabled; move constructor and move assignment are implemented and tested (moved-from object becomes empty).
No raw `fclose`/`delete` calls occur outside the RAII type; resource release is centralized.
Demo writes some bytes to a file, then throws; after catching, subsequent open of the same file path succeeds and the program prints a line confirming closure.
Buildable with a single compiler command shown in README (e.g., `g++ -std=c++17 demo.cpp -o demo`).
`output.txt` includes two runs: normal flow and throwing flow, each indicating whether the file was closed (e.g., via printed messages).

rubric.criterion: Correct RAII implementation: destructor closes exactly once; no leaks or double-closes in normal and exceptional paths.
Move-only semantics implemented correctly and demonstrated (tests show moved-from is safe to destroy/use).
Exception safety demonstration: program throws after an operation and still closes the file; evidence present in output.
Submission quality: clear README with build/run steps; compiles cleanly; no raw manual closes outside the wrapper.

practical_tasks.title: Container application: Word frequency with map, set, and iterators
practical_tasks.brief: Implement a console tool that reads text from stdin, counts word frequencies case-insensitively while excluding stopwords, and prints the top N words in descending frequency then ascending lexicographic order. Use `std::map` for counts, `std::set` for stopwords, and a `std::vector` to sort the results for output. Demonstrate correct iterator use (no invalidation bugs) and stable behavior.
practical_tasks.deliverable: Source files (e.g., `main.cpp`) and `README.md` with build/run instructions. Include a sample input file `sample.txt` and the exact captured output in `expected_output.txt` produced by running `./app < sample.txt 10` (N=10).

concept_mcqs.explanation: std::remove_if compacts the kept elements (odds) to the front and returns an iterator to the new logical end. For the vector {1,2,3,4,5,6} with predicate removing evens, the new end is at index 3, so it - begin() prints 3. After erase, the vector contains {1,3,5}, so the final output is "3 135".
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: 6 is the original size, but remove_if returns the new logical end, not the container size. C: After erase, the vector no longer contains all elements; remove_if leaves garbage in the tail which must be erased. D: 153 suggests the odds were reordered; remove_if preserves the relative order of kept elements.

options: It depends on the implementation but usually 1
Undefined behavior
concept_mcqs.explanation: binary_search requires the range to be sorted according to the same comparator it uses. The vector is sorted in descending order but binary_search uses operator< (ascending), so the precondition is violated and the algorithm will return an incorrect result. In this concrete case it prints 0 (not found).
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Tempting because 3 is in the data, but the range is sorted with a different ordering, so the search fails. C: The behavior is not undefined; the algorithm may return an arbitrary boolean, but it stays within the algorithm’s logic. D: Not implementation-defined; the mismatch in ordering means success is not guaranteed and in this case is false.

concept_mcqs.explanation: stable_partition groups negatives first while preserving the original relative order within each group. The negatives in their original order are -1, -7, -3; the non-negatives in their original order are 3, 2, 5. So the final sequence is "-1 -7 -3 3 2 5 ".
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Looks sorted among negatives, but stable_partition does not sort either group. C and D: Both break the original relative order either among negatives or among non-negatives; stability guarantees preservation within groups.

concept_mcqs.explanation: nth_element arranges the element at the nth position as if the range were sorted, and partitions the range so that elements before are <= it and elements after are >= it. It does not sort either partition. For this input, v[4] becomes 5, and the subranges are not necessarily sorted, hence both flags print 0.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B and C: Common misconception that nth_element sorts the left partition; it only partially orders. D: The median position is correctly placed at 5 for this permutation; 4 is incorrect.

options: Undefined behavior
concept_mcqs.explanation: equal_range on a sorted range returns the subrange of all elements equal to the value. There are three 2's in the input, so the distance between the bounds is 3.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Off-by-one temptation. C: Counts all elements up to 3, but equal_range isolates equals only. D: The preconditions (sorted ascending with operator<) are met; behavior is well-defined.

options: Using pivot is safe if push_back adds at most one element.
Using pivot is always safe because partition doesn't change capacity.
Using pivot after push_back is undefined behavior because it may be invalidated by reallocation.
Using pivot is safe because partition returns an index, not an iterator.
concept_mcqs.explanation: std::vector reallocation invalidates all iterators, including ones returned by algorithms like partition. After a potential reallocation from push_back, using pivot is undefined behavior.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: partition’s behavior on capacity is irrelevant; push_back may reallocate regardless. C: Even a single-element growth can reallocate and invalidate iterators. D: partition returns an iterator, not an index; iterators are invalidated on reallocation.

concept_mcqs.explanation: The callable multiplies 1 by 10, then throws on 2 before modifying it. The third element is never visited. After catching, the vector is {10,2,3}.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Assumes the second element was modified before throwing. C: Assumes no elements were modified; for_each does not roll back. D: Assumes the third element was processed; iteration stops at the throw.

options: First line contains C (copies), second line contains m (moves).
Both lines contain M (moves).
First line contains M (moves), second line contains c (copies).
Both lines contain c (copies).
concept_mcqs.explanation: On reallocation, vector prefers move if it is noexcept; otherwise it falls back to copy for strong exception safety. MoveNoexcept moves (prints M). MoveMayThrow’s move may throw, so vector copies (prints c).
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Inverts the noexcept rule. C and D: Assume the same behavior regardless of noexcept; vector’s guarantee drives the choice.

options: A fails; B compiles.
Both fail because iterator_category is not usable in enable_if.
Both A and B compile.
A compiles; B fails.
concept_mcqs.explanation: std::vector’s iterator_category is std::random_access_iterator_tag, so A satisfies the equality check. std::list uses std::bidirectional_iterator_tag, so B fails the enable_if. Using is_same is strict but works for vector iterators; a more general approach would use is_base_of.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Lists are not random-access. C: Inverts the categories. D: iterator_category is exactly intended for such traits-based constraints; SFINAE with enable_if is valid.

options: Undefined behavior
base
Nothing; the exception is swallowed by transform
derived
concept_mcqs.explanation: Catch blocks are matched in order. The base-class handler catches MyError before the derived one is considered. Algorithms do not swallow exceptions; they propagate them out to the caller.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Tempting because the thrown type is MyError, but the base handler appears first and matches. C: Standard algorithms do not catch and suppress exceptions from user callables. D: There is no undefined behavior here; exception flow is well defined.

practical_tasks.brief: Create a small, header-only library that provides two generic algorithms: 1) top_k(first,last,k,comp) returning a vector of the k largest elements by comparator without fully sorting, and 2) median_inplace(first,last,comp) that positions the median via nth_element. top_k must validate k (0 <= k <= n) and throw std::invalid_argument on bad k. Provide overloads that accept containers by reference and forward to iterator-based implementations. Include a minimal demo program that exercises both utilities on ints and strings and prints results.
practical_tasks.deliverable: A header file (e.g., algoutils.hpp) plus a demo source that compiles and runs to show correctness. This serves as the "Reusable component" completion evidence.
acceptance_criteria: Header-only: No compiled library; all templates in headers.
top_k uses nth_element (or partial_sort) to achieve O(n + k log k) or O(n log k) behavior; document the chosen complexity in comments.
top_k validates k and throws std::invalid_argument for k < 0 or k > distance(first,last). The demo must show the exception being thrown and caught, printing the exception message exactly: "bad k".

Iterator constraints: Both functions reject non-random-access iterators at compile-time using iterator_category and enable_if or static_assert with a clear message.

Demo output includes: a) top 3 strings by length, b) top 5 integers by natural order, c) thrown exception for bad k with the exact message, and d) a median example with left/right partitions not fully sorted.
Builds with: g++ -std=c++17 demo.cpp -O2, and the demo prints clear, labeled results.

options: In the constructor `std::ifstream in(...)`, because failed opens throw by default.
No exception is thrown; streams never throw on open failures.
On the call to `in.exceptions(...)`, because `failbit` was already set by the failed open and enabling it triggers a throw immediately.
On the call to `std::getline(in, s)`, because that's the first formatted operation after enabling exceptions.
concept_mcqs.explanation: `std::ifstream("missing.txt")` fails to open and sets `failbit`. When you call `exceptions(failbit|badbit)`, the standard requires it to throw immediately if any of the bits being enabled are already set. Hence the throw occurs on `exceptions(...)`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Many believe failed opens throw by default, but streams are non-throwing unless exceptions are enabled. C: Reasonable guess because formatted ops typically surface errors, but here the throw occurs earlier when enabling exceptions. D: Streams can throw, but only when exceptions are enabled; here they are, and the state is already failed.

options: [alpha] [beta]
[ ] [alpha]
[ ] [beta]
[alpha] [ ]
concept_mcqs.explanation: After `in >> n`, the newline remains in the stream. The first `getline` consumes just that newline, yielding an empty `line1`. The second `getline` then reads "alpha" into `line2`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Assumes `getline` skips the remaining newline automatically; it does not. C/D: Each mixes up which call sees the newline versus the next line.

options: Open the streams in text mode by removing `std::ios::binary`.
Trim `\r` manually after `getline` using `if (!line.empty() && line.back()=='\r') line.pop_back();`.
Call `std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false);` before I/O.
Use `std::getline(in >> std::ws, line)` to consume whitespace including `\r`.
concept_mcqs.explanation:
In text mode on Windows, the runtime translates `
` to `
` during input, and `getline` strips the `
`, avoiding stray ``. Opening in binary mode disables translation and leaves `` in the buffer.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Works but adds logic instead of fixing the mode that caused the problem; the question asks for a minimal change to I/O behavior. C: `std::ws` does not affect `getline` nor strip `\r` before it; `getline` reads until `\n`. D: Syncing with stdio only affects coordination with C I/O; it does nothing to CRLF translation.

concept_mcqs.stem:
This project builds a library `util` and an app `app`:

```text
add_library(util src/util.cpp)
target_include_directories(util PRIVATE ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/include)

add_executable(app src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE util)
```
`src/main.cpp` includes `#include <util/format.h>` located in `include/util/format.h`. The build fails for `app` with "file not found". What single change fixes it without adding include dirs to `app`?
options: Change `target_include_directories(util PRIVATE ...)` to `PUBLIC`.
Add `include_directories(${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/include)` at the top level.
Change `target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE util)` to `PUBLIC`.
Set `CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20` for both targets.
concept_mcqs.explanation: `#include` paths are usage requirements. Marking the include dir `PUBLIC` on `util` propagates it to link dependents like `app`. Keeping it `PRIVATE` hides the header path from `app`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Link visibility (`PRIVATE`/`PUBLIC`) here controls propagation of compile/link usage requirements from `util` to `app`, but changing the linkage on `app` doesn't export headers out of `util`. C: Works, but global include dirs are a step backward; the minimal, modern fix is to declare proper usage requirements. D: Language standard does not affect header search paths.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You rebase a feature branch and try to push:

```text
A---B---C  origin/main
         \
          D---E   origin/feature

# local
$ git checkout feature
$ git rebase origin/main
# history becomes linear locally
A---B---C---D'---E'

$ git push origin feature
# rejected: non-fast-forward
```
You want to update the remote `feature` with your rebased commits while protecting teammates against accidental overwrites. What is the next command?
options:
```bash
git push --force-with-lease origin feature
```

```bash
git pull --rebase origin feature && git push origin feature
```

```bash
git merge origin/main && git push origin feature
```

```bash
git push origin feature
```
concept_mcqs.explanation: After a rebase, the remote needs a forced update; `--force-with-lease` is the safe variant that refuses to overwrite remote changes you don't have locally.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Merging after a rebase defeats the purpose and still won't fast-forward the remote feature to your rewritten history. C: Repeating the same push won't change the non-fast-forward error. D: Pulling won't reconcile your rewritten local history with the remote without a force push.

concept_mcqs.stem:
On Windows with the Visual Studio generator, you configure, build Release, then run tests:

```bash
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build --config Release
ctest --test-dir build
```
CTest runs Debug binaries by default and several performance tests are slow. How do you run the Release tests without reconfiguring?
options:
```bash
ctest --use-release
```

```bash
ctest --test-dir build -C Release
```

```bash
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
```

```bash
ctest --build-config Release
```
concept_mcqs.explanation: Multi-config generators select the configuration at build and test time with `--config`/`-C`. `ctest -C Release` selects the Release artifacts for execution.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: There is no `--build-config` flag in CTest. C: `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` is ignored by multi-config generators; and you don't need to reconfigure. D: Not a real CTest option.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A test reads a bundled resource:

```cpp
// tests/reader_test.cpp
std::ifstream in("data/sample.txt");
REQUIRE(in.good());
```
`sample.txt` lives at `${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/tests/data/sample.txt`. Locally it passes, but on CI CTest runs from the build tree and the test fails to find the file.

CMake:

```text
add_executable(reader tests/reader_test.cpp src/reader.cpp)
add_test(NAME reader COMMAND reader)
```
What is the best fix that keeps tests hermetic and does not bake source-tree paths into the binary?
options:
```cpp
// Hardcode in code
auto p = std::string("${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/tests/data/sample.txt");
std::ifstream in(p);
```
```text
# CMake
configure_file(${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/tests/data/sample.txt
               ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/data/sample.txt COPYONLY)
# test code keeps: std::ifstream in("data/sample.txt");
```
```cpp
// Test code at runtime
chdir("/absolute/path/to/source"); // set working dir to source tree
```
```text
Rely on the IDE to set the test's working directory to tests/.
```
concept_mcqs.explanation: Copying resources to the binary dir at configure/build time and reading them via a relative path keeps tests hermetic and independent of the source layout. It works the same under CTest on CI.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B/D: Baking absolute source paths makes binaries non-portable and breaks in packaged/test environments. C: IDE-specific behavior is not reliable on CI.

options: Replace the assert with `if (!p) return 0;` for all cases.
Compile Release with `-UNDEBUG` so asserts stay enabled.
Keep the assert and change the test.

Replace the assert with an explicit check that allows `nullptr` only when `n==0`, otherwise guards:
```cpp
if (!p) { if (n==0) return 0; else throw std::invalid_argument("p"); }
```
concept_mcqs.explanation: `assert` is removed in Release, so dereferencing through `p` can crash. Enforcing the contract at runtime with a conditional that permits `nullptr` only when `n==0` preserves behavior across build types.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Silently accepting `nullptr` even when `n>0` weakens the contract. B: The test captures a real requirement; build-type-sensitive logic is a bug. D: Keeping asserts in Release is not a robust contract mechanism, and many toolchains don't recommend it.

concept_mcqs.stem:
CTest discovers no tests:

```text
add_executable(tests unit/test_main.cpp)
enable_testing()
# ctest -N prints: "No tests were found."
```
What is the minimal change to make `ctest -N` list a test and allow `ctest` to run it?
options:
```text
set(BUILD_TESTING ON)
```

```text
include(CTest)
```

```text
add_executable(test unit/test_main.cpp) # rename target to 'test'
```

```text
add_test(NAME unit COMMAND tests)
```
concept_mcqs.explanation: CTest only runs tests that are registered with `add_test`. Enabling testing without registering any tests still yields zero tests.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B/D: `include(CTest)` and `BUILD_TESTING` control whether testing is enabled, not whether any specific test exists. C: Target names don't matter to CTest unless you register them.

options: Check `if (in.fail() && !in.eof())`.
Use `if (in.good())` to report success.
Use `if (in.bad())` to report actual I/O errors only.
Report success if `in.gcount() > 0`.
concept_mcqs.explanation: After `read`, a short read sets `failbit` and possibly `eofbit`, but not `badbit`. Testing `bad()` detects true I/O failures and ignores expected short reads at EOF.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Also correct in spirit for many cases, but it conflates `failbit` set for formatting vs. raw reads and is more verbose than needed here. C: `gcount()>0` doesn't detect a mid-stream I/O error that still delivered some bytes. D: `good()` will be false for short reads at EOF, making it unsuitable if short reads are intended to be non-errors.

scenario_questions.scenario: Your test `Reader.CanOpenBundledSample` passes locally but fails on CI. The test opens `data/sample.txt` with `std::ifstream in("data/sample.txt");` and asserts `in.good()`. Under CTest, the working directory is the build tree and the file lives in `${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/tests/data/sample.txt`. The project uses CMake and runs `ctest -j` on CI.
scenario_questions.task: Propose a fix that makes the test hermetic and portable across platforms and build layouts. Justify your choice versus two alternatives you reject. Provide any required CMake and minimal code changes.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
A robust fix is to copy test resources into the binary dir and reference them via a path relative to the test’s working directory or pass the path as a test argument.

One minimal pattern:

CMake at configure/build time:
```text
# CMakeLists.txt in the test directory
file(MAKE_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/data)
configure_file(${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/data/sample.txt
               ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/data/sample.txt COPYONLY)
add_executable(reader tests/reader_test.cpp src/reader.cpp)
add_test(NAME reader COMMAND reader)
```

Test code remains:
```cpp
std::ifstream in("data/sample.txt");
REQUIRE(in.good());
```

Alternatively, make the path explicit via `add_test` arguments:
```text
add_test(NAME reader COMMAND reader ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/data/sample.txt)
```

and in code:
```cpp
int main(int argc, char** argv){
  std::filesystem::path p = argc>1 ? argv[1] : "data/sample.txt";
  std::ifstream in(p);
  REQUIRE(in.good());
}
```

Why this is preferred: it avoids baking source-tree absolute paths into the binary (portable, works in install trees and CI), avoids IDE-only working directory assumptions, and plays well with parallel `ctest -j` because each test uses its own binary dir.

Rejected alternatives:
- Hardcoding `${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}` in the binary (breaks relocatability, fails in packaged or install tests).
- `chdir` to the source directory in the test (test becomes environment-dependent and violates hermeticity).

rubric.criterion: Identifies working-directory mismatch under CTest as the root cause
Proposes a hermetic solution (copy resource to binary dir or pass binary-dir path) with correct CMake commands
Shows minimal code change to consume the resource path (or none if using relative path post-copy)
Justifies choice versus at least two concrete, inferior alternatives

scenario_questions.scenario: You are asked to build a small CLI that summarizes a large CSV log (gigabytes). The current proof-of-concept reads the entire file into a `std::string`, splits, and times out; tests are slow and flaky.
scenario_questions.task: Propose an architecture and build layout that streams the file, is unit-testable, and supports fast tests. Provide component boundaries, how you inject dependencies for tests, and the CMake target structure. Justify how your design enables debugging and performance investigation.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
Architecture:
- `ILogReader` interface (pure C++) with `bool next(Row&);` implemented by `CsvStreamReader` that wraps an `std::istream&` and parses rows incrementally.
- `Aggregator` that consumes `Row`s and updates statistics. No I/O inside; pure logic functions to ease testing.
- `main` wires `std::ifstream` to `CsvStreamReader` and the `Aggregator`. CLI parses `--file` and parameters.

Dependency injection for tests:
- Provide `MockReader` that returns canned rows from a `std::vector<Row>`. Unit tests cover edge cases without touching the filesystem.
- For file I/O tests, open small temp files via `std::filesystem::temp_directory_path()` and run targeted integration tests.

CMake layout:
```text
add_library(csvcore
    src/csv_stream_reader.cpp
    src/aggregator.cpp)
target_include_directories(csvcore PUBLIC include)

add_executable(csvsummarize src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(csvsummarize PRIVATE csvcore)

# Tests
add_executable(csv_tests tests/aggregator_tests.cpp tests/reader_tests.cpp)
target_link_libraries(csv_tests PRIVATE csvcore)
add_test(NAME csv_tests COMMAND csv_tests)
```

Testing strategy:
- Unit tests hit `Aggregator` with synthetic rows (milliseconds runtime).
- Reader tests feed tiny in-memory streams using `std::istringstream` to avoid disk.
- A single integration test with a small on-disk CSV verifies the plumbing; resource copied to binary dir via `configure_file`.

Debugging and perf:
- Add `--profile` flag to emit counts and processing rate periodically; guard behind runtime flag to keep tests stable.
- Structure code so `Aggregator` is trivially benchmarkable with synthetic data; add `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo` for CI perf runs and use `ctest -C RelWithDebInfo`.
- Log parse errors with row/column indices; make parse error handling injectable (strategy pattern) to test failure paths deterministically.

rubric.criterion: Streams-based design that avoids loading full file and cleanly separates parsing from aggregation
Clear testability plan (mocks/in-memory streams) and minimal use of filesystem in unit tests
CMake target structure with library/executable split and proper include/link usage
Debugging/performance considerations (flags, profiling hooks, reproducibility) with concrete steps

scenario_questions.scenario: Your CLI `tool --version` must print the project version. Requirement: use Git tags when available (e.g., `v1.2.3-4-gabcdef`), else fall back to the CMake project version. Releases are tagged on `main`. CI builds on Linux and Windows.
scenario_questions.task: Design a cross-platform solution that embeds the version into the binary at build time and outline the Git release steps. Provide the necessary CMake snippet and explain how your approach behaves in a shallow clone or on a developer machine without Git.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
Approach: query Git at configure time and generate a header with a macro, with a robust fallback.

CMake:
```text
# Try to get a Git description
find_package(Git QUIET)
set(PROJECT_SEMVER ${PROJECT_VERSION})
set(GIT_DESC "")
if (Git_FOUND)
  execute_process(
    COMMAND ${GIT_EXECUTABLE} describe --tags --dirty --always
    WORKING_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}
    RESULT_VARIABLE GIT_DESCR_OK
    OUTPUT_VARIABLE GIT_DESC
    OUTPUT_STRIP_TRAILING_WHITESPACE)
endif()
if (NOT GIT_DESCR_OK EQUAL 0 OR GIT_DESC STREQUAL "")
  set(GIT_DESC ${PROJECT_SEMVER})
endif()
configure_file(${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/cmake/version.h.in
               ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/generated/version.h @ONLY)

# Consumers
target_include_directories(app PRIVATE ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/generated)
```

`version.h.in`:
```cpp
#pragma once
#define APP_VERSION "@GIT_DESC@"
```

Runtime:
```cpp
std::cout << APP_VERSION << "\n";
```

Behavior without Git or in shallow clones: `git describe` fails; the code falls back to `PROJECT_VERSION`. Works on Windows and Linux (no POSIX-only tools).

Git release steps:
- Ensure `main` is green on CI.
- Bump `project(VERSION x.y.z)` if needed; commit.
- Tag: `git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "Release vX.Y.Z" && git push --tags`.
- Build on CI; binaries will embed the tag (e.g., `vX.Y.Z`).
- Post-release: branch cuts (if applicable) and changelog update in a follow-up commit.

Optional: add a CTest that invokes the binary and checks `APP_VERSION` contains either a tag-like string or `PROJECT_VERSION`.

practical_tasks.title: Build a tested file I/O utility: uniqcount
practical_tasks.brief: Implement a small command-line utility `uniqcount` that reads a UTF-8 text file and reports the number of total lines, number of non-empty lines, and the top N most frequent non-empty lines. Provide focused unit tests around parsing and counting, including platform newline differences.
practical_tasks.deliverable: A folder `uniqcount/` containing C++ source, CMakeLists.txt, tests, and a short README. The assessor will run: `cmake -S uniqcount -B build && cmake --build build && ctest --test-dir build` and `build/uniqcount --file sample.txt --top 3`.
acceptance_criteria: Builds with CMake on Linux and Windows using `cmake -S uniqcount -B build && cmake --build build` without editing files.

Running `build/uniqcount --file sample.txt --top 3` prints a single line of JSON to stdout with keys total_lines, non_empty_lines, top (array of {line,count}), in deterministic order for ties (lexicographic).
